*Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa says she has not spoken with Elon Musk but is open to working with him after he described her as “quite moderate” and predicted she would be “fine” as governor.*

• *Musk:* Hinojosa acknowledged his significant business interests in Texas and said cooperation must benefit Texans.
• *Political Identity:* Asked whether she is a moderate, Hinojosa rejected ideological labels, saying, “If I had to label myself, I'd call myself an economic populist.”
• *Corporate Influence:* She argued that corporate interests have corrupted both political parties and called for leaders who prioritize constituents over corporate pressure.
• *Economic Priorities:* Hinojosa said Texas can maintain a strong business community, but its economy must serve residents first.

Lumentum *($LITE)* CEO Michael Hurlston defended its planned $115B all-stock merger with Marvell *($MRVL)* after shares plunged 42% and 45%, respectively, since Oct. 28, acknowledging shareholder frustration but citing strong AI demand.

• *Deal Outlook:* Announced Nov. 2, the merger is expected to close in H1 2028. The $115B figure represented Lumentum’s implied enterprise value at announcement.
• *Growth Driver:* Hurlston sees the shift from copper to fiber-optic connections inside AI data centers as a major opportunity, with no slowdown in Lumentum’s demand.
• *Investor Concerns:* Both stocks have suffered from merger skepticism and broader AI valuation pressure. Hurlston acknowledged, “We’ve got work to do with our shareholders.”
• *Upcoming Catalysts:* Marvell’s Dec. 1 earnings, the merger’s S-4 filing and Lumentum’s next earnings report could help rebuild investor confidence.
• *Financial Strength:* Lumentum’s latest quarterly revenue more than doubled year over year, beating expectations. Hurlston said both businesses are performing strongly.

SpaceX lenders sought to prevent Elon Musk from launching Nvidia *($NVDA)* AI chips securing a $43B debt package into orbit, fearing the collateral would be impossible to recover in a default, according to people familiar with the deal.

• *Project Saturn:* SpaceX sold more than $30B in debt Thursday, including $25B in investment-grade bonds backed by five-year lease payments on Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs.
• *Orbital Restrictions:* Lenders proposed prohibiting the launch of pledged chips as Musk pursues space-based AI data centers. It remains unclear whether the restriction was included in final documents.
• *Bond Terms:* The $25B tranche carries an estimated 8.3% yield, or 3.45 percentage points above Treasuries. Bonds mature in 2032, with principal scheduled for repayment in under four years.
• *Credit Structure:* Debt was issued through a special-purpose vehicle to preserve SpaceX’s investment-grade rating. Moody’s rated the debt A3 and KBRA A-, supported by binding lease payments.
• *Investors:* Pimco committed $4B, with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR also participating. Apollo and Goldman Sachs led the deal.
• *Deployment:* Moody’s says the GPUs are intended for SpaceX-controlled U.S. data centers on Earth, not orbital facilities.

*Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa reaffirmed plans to ban new data center permits when she takes office in January, clarifying that projects already approved would not be frozen.*

• *Moratorium:* Hinojosa told Bret Baier she would block new permits within her authority until Texas passes stronger protections for residents.
• *Industry Position:* “I don't hate data centers; I just hate the way they're taking advantage of Texans right now.”
• *Existing Projects:* “I don't think I have power to stop what's already been done,” she said, distinguishing previously approved projects from pending applications.
• *Local Control:* Hinojosa wants communities to have a say in whether and how data centers are built near them.
• ⁠*The proposal comes as Texas regulators have resumed issuing data center air permits ahead of her inauguration.*

*Multiple cyberattacks and data breaches were reported worldwide Thursday, Nov. 19, as the NSA’s classified communications network remained disrupted for a third day. U.S. officials say there is no evidence linking the NSA outage to a cyberattack or the recent wave of infrastructure failures.*

• *NSA Network:* NSANet disruptions affected intelligence operations supporting the Middle East, forcing personnel to use backup communications. Officials attributed the outage to software updates, not malicious activity.
• *U.S. Banking:* JPMorgan Chase *($JPM)*, Visa *($V)* and Mastercard *($MA)* disclosed cyberattacks involving third-party vendors that exposed some customer information. Their core payment networks were not compromised.
• *Nvidia:* *($NVDA)* is investigating claims by the Gentlemen ransomware group, which threatened to release data Nov. 28. Nvidia found no evidence its own networks were breached but is investigating a possible third-party incident.
• *European Commission:* Officials confirmed an AI-assisted cyberattack targeting internal systems. The investigation remains ongoing.
• *Norwegian Energy:* Equinor confirmed its cyberattack remained ongoing Thursday, while Skagerak Energi separately reported an attempted intrusion. Energy production was unaffected.
• *VMware:* Google researchers disclosed Chinese-linked exploitation of a critical vCenter vulnerability dating to September. Broadcom issued emergency patches Thursday.
• *Additional Breaches:* Japan’s SBC Medical Group disclosed exposure of 1.6M customer records, while Ethiopian Airlines investigated a breach involving its ShebaMiles loyalty program.

*Global markets extended their selloff into Friday’s Asian session, with Japan and South Korea plunging over 4%, gold falling below $3,550, silver below $42 and Bitcoin nearing $61,000. Rising Fed rate-hike expectations, AI valuation concerns and broad risk reduction are intensifying pressure across asset classes.*

• *U.S. Markets:* The Dow plunged 1,101 points Thursday to 49,097, its first close below 50,000 since June. The S&P 500 lost 2.02% and Nasdaq fell 2.25%, despite Anthropic’s record IPO.
• *Asian Selloff:* Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s KOSPI dropped over 4%. SoftBank plunged roughly 16%, while SK Hynix and Samsung fell sharply as selling spread across AI and semiconductor stocks.
• *Gold & Silver:* Precious metals extended their decline to multimonth lows. A stronger dollar, expectations of further Fed tightening and possible margin-related selling are outweighing safe-haven demand.
• *Bitcoin:* BTC traded near $61,700 as U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs continued experiencing withdrawals. Funds recorded $306.5M in net outflows Nov. 18, including $148.7M from BlackRock’s IBIT.
• *Federal Reserve:* Markets are pricing another December rate hike following hawkish Fed minutes. The dollar reached a 19-month high, increasing pressure on non-yielding assets and leveraged investments.

*White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired, CBS News reports, contradicting earlier accounts describing his departure as amicable. The dismissal comes amid widespread U.S. technology outages and growing concerns about cybersecurity readiness.*

• *Dismissal:* White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller reportedly wanted Cairncross removed from his first day in the role, questioning whether he had the cybersecurity expertise needed for the position.
• *Replacement:* Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will replace Cairncross. Reuters reports she will initially serve in an acting capacity.
• *Infrastructure Outages:* The departure follows disruptions affecting Microsoft, air traffic control, banks and the NSA. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators found no evidence the outages were connected and was “98% confident” they were not caused by malicious foreign activity.

*The U.S. Senate just passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) in a 62–33 vote Thursday, advancing a major overhaul of federal energy permitting aimed at accelerating power generation, transmission infrastructure and grid expansion as AI data center electricity demand surges.*

• *Faster Permitting:* The bill streamlines federal environmental reviews for power plants, transmission lines, pipelines and other infrastructure, while reducing many legal challenge windows to 150 days.
• *Data Center Costs:* New data centers of all sizes would be required to cover the additional grid infrastructure costs they create, rather than passing those expenses to households and other electricity customers.
• *Financial Protections:* Data center operators would face financial guarantees and continued payment obligations to protect ratepayers if facilities shut down before related infrastructure costs are recovered.
• *Power Grid Expansion:* Federal regulators would gain broader authority to approve certain interstate transmission lines, potentially accelerating electricity delivery to AI campuses and other high-demand regions.
• *Community Oversight:* The bill would establish federal technical assistance for local governments evaluating data center electricity demand, water use, infrastructure costs and economic impacts.
• *White House Support:* Trump endorsed BAAJA as advancing his “America First Energy Agenda,” while the White House formally declared strong support for its passage and recommended presidential approval.
• *Next Steps:* The Senate-amended bill heads to the House, which must approve the same text before it reaches Trump for his signature.
